utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom this afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, again, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, together with my colleagues, Ms. April Carter and Ms. Carolyn Edgerton, and our case manager, Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Novak Lukic and Gregor Guy-Smith for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I guess, Mr. Saxon, you can call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unless you have any housekeeping matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If Mr. van Lynden could return to the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May Mr. van Lynden be brought in the court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting, just to avoid some confusion later on in the session, I believe I will only need about half an hour more to complete my direct examination. The Prosecution has calculated that so far I have used 110 minutes, or just under two hours. I hope that is roughly equivalent to what the Registry has calculated as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may very well be aware of this, but it's still my duty to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the commencement of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. van Lynden. Just to clarify one matter, several times on Friday when I asked you about the forces in Sarajevo opposing the Bosnian Serb army, you referred to the "Bosnian army."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This was at pages 471 and 478 of the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is, did the Bosnian Serb army have a more formal name, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I imagine it was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I should maybe add in this context that that army had not existed at the beginning of 1992, and it was only being -- a fledgling force, so to speak, and initially it could be quite confusing when one was in Sarajevo as to where members -- were people member of the Territorial Defence or of the army or simply of militias that had sprung up in defence of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, is the answer to your question, sir, the short answer, that by "Bosnian Serb army" you were referring to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what has been written here. This is what I thought I heard you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question referred to the forces in Sarajevo opposing the Bosnian -- you're absolutely right, Your Honour. It was my mistake in the transcript, and the question should read, at line 23: Did the Bosnian army have a more formal name? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And your response to that, Mr. van Lynden, was the formal name was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? We need an oral answer.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it also known at times by an acronym or an abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The acronym I'm aware of is ABiH, armija Bosnia i Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When we stopped on Friday, we had seen a new report that you did for SkyNews of an interview with Ratko Mladic. When you met General Mladic in September 1992, was he cordial to you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Subsequently, did you and your SkyNews team do any reports about the place near Sarajevo called Zuc?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is a hill to the north of the Sarajevo; and yes, in December 1992, we did a report after Zuc was captured by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for the record the witness drew the rough location of Zuc on the image that has been MFIed as P1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for purposes of clarification so I understand where we stand when we're discussing the Bosnian army, I understand that we're now discussing the army that has the acronym of ABiH? Is that the world in which we're in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I'm trying to find out, just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that your understanding as well, Mr. van Lynden? By "the Bosnian army," you're referring to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'm grateful to Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In December 1992, you mentioned that Zuc was captured by the Bosnian army, or the ABiH. Did you and your team do a report about the events at Zuc at that time?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you and your SkyNews team do any reports about a place called Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, various reports initially from Sarajevo, using ham radio operators, but later, at the beginning of 1993, we actually went to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where was Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Gorazde is in eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and is it -- can you recall approximately the distance between Sarajevo and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine. Was there something significant about Gorazde at that time?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Gorazde was one of the besieged enclaves of eastern Bosnia, like Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you manage to enter Gorazde and report about the situation there?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We discovered in early February 1993 that there was a track through the Serb lines across the mountains from the Gorazde enclave to a Bosnian army base camp and that up to 500 people a night were taking this trail to get food from the Bosnian army camp and then bring it back to Gorazde. We did a report about that, and ten days or maybe two weeks later we took that trail ourselves and went to Gorazde for -- and stayed there for about two or two and a half weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during those two to two and a half weeks, did you produce reports about the situation in Gorazde that were subsequently broadcast on SkyNews?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, after you did your reports about the events in Zuc and about the Gorazde safe haven, did you ever have further contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I encountered General Mladic again at the building that was known as the Bosnian Serb Presidency in Pale in February 1994 ahead of a meeting between -- which Mr. Mladic was attending with Radovan Karadzic and others of the Bosnian Serb command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, how did General Mladic treat you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In a rather unfriendly manner. The general was not particularly happy to see me and made that very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He grabbed me with one hand in my face and spat out the words "Zuc" and "Gorazde." For the rest, I didn't know what he was saying. I didn't have my producer with me at that particular moment. The only other person that was there was John Simpson of the BBC. But it was clear that the General was not happy with my reporting either about Zuc or about Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't have your interpreter with you, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My producers were my interpreters, Your Honour, and the producer I had with me at the time was a man called Jaksa Scekic, and he was a separate room with the cameraman because we had been told that we would probably get an interview, and we had expected to do an interview with Mr. Karadzic. As it turned out, the BBC and SkyNews were invited simply to film the beginning of the meeting of the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, them. To the extent that the witness is making a conclusion about why General Mladic was displeased to see him, I would object on the grounds of speculation because he did not have any information other than the names of two places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it would seem fairly conclusory if someone grabs you by the face and spits out the names of two places about which you had recently done some television reporting, clearly the nature of that person's feelings would be fairly obvious. That is the Prosecution's position. This is not speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one more piece of SkyNews footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is from 65 ter number 4346, footage that was shot December 1992. We will not show the entire clip. We will begin it at 48 seconds, and then we will stop at 1 minute and 34 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We are not getting any sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: GENERAL: "All of the Security Council resolutions, all of these local agreement, all of these effort we are making here to improve the situation and to save the lives and to restore the capability of the utilities for the winter is completely held and we move one step forward, and we find ourselves two steps back."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, can you recall who this person speaking was? We're at 1:34 of the video.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was the general commanding the Egyptian battalion within UNPROFOR, and they and him were based in Sarajevo. And this is, as I recall, at the PTT, the UN headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we heard references from the Egyptian general to comments like "one step forward, two steps back." What was he referring to? What was the topic that he was discussing?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The general situation in Bosnia and in Sarajevo in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please, until we stop at 1 minute, 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: REPORTER: "... in the city. Serb and incendiary rounds setting a string of flats ablaze in one apartment block. A resident watches, distraught, his home and belongings gone. Seconds later, further bursts of incendiary rounds crash into the building or bounce off the wall into ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We stopped now just a bit over --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters be given the references for the transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, and I apologise because I should have given this previously. The ERN of the English transcript is 0304-3961 to 0304-3961; for the B/C/S, it is 0304-3930-0304-3931.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We stopped here at a minute, 55 seconds point 7. In the middle of the screen, we see a reddish object. Can you tell us what that reddish object is?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's an incendiary round that had hit the apartment block and then bounced back literally over the heads of my cameraman and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: REPORTER: "... street below. Wanton arson on a purely civilian target. As ever, Sarajevo's remarkable firemen fight back, getting their hoses to the flames for once unhampered by a cut in the water supply, but for the fire chief, water is not the main concern. His engines are running out of fuel, and he tells us he won't be able to cope with another fire this day. The fall of [indiscernible] escalation of shelling here in the centre of Sarajevo, again on the line, the impotence of international efforts in Bosnia. Cease-fires and political talks have led nowhere and won't until the western world proves it has a true commitment in ending this war. Aernout van Lynden, SkyNews, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, who is this person we see speaking here?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you observe any outgoing fire from that building that day, the building that was being struck by incendiary rounds?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about the surrounding area? Any outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We did not see any, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you make any inquiries to see if anyone else observed outgoing fire from that building or that area?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Firstly, with the people like the man that you saw earlier in the report who had -- whose apartment was on fire. We asked him and other residents whether that building had been used by the Bosnian army or anyone armed to fire on the opposing side, and they said -- initially, they literally said to us, Do you think we're mad? We would know the consequences, and no, it hasn't. But we checked up afterwards or so. We went to the UNPROFOR headquarters and checked with UNPROFOR officers, and they had noted the fire, and they had said that on that occasion at that location there had only been incoming fire and no outgoing fire. That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Apart from the incendiary rounds that struck that apartment building, did you observe any other kind of shell or ammunition striking that building?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was that significant to you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was. It was for me the first instance that I saw of just incendiary rounds being used. I should maybe also add that having served in the Dutch military and having witnessed western armies during the Gulf War, these are armies that don't have incendiary rounds, but the Yugoslav Army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you observe firefighters enter that apartment building that day?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did anything happen after the firefighters entered that caught your attention?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There were fires on various floors, but they tried to -- and they tried to fight them on various floors. But one of the fires was right at the top of the building, and we noticed that once the firefighters had reached the upper floors of the building, more rounds came in but now aimed at the lower part of the apartment block, which indicated to us that the firefighters had been spotted and that the people shooting at the apartment block were really trying to cut off their way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this video-clip now along with its transcripts, which would be 65 ter 4341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video-clip together with its transcripts is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just for purposes of clarification - I may have missed it - what is the date of this video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I believe the witness may be able to tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall the date, Mr. van Lynden, when this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do. It was the -- actually, the 5th of December, 1992. In an original statement, I had said either the end of November or early December. Later on, my memory recalled that this was the 5th of December because the 5th of December is a special date within the Netherlands of St. Nicholas, and I recall calling my family, my children, later that day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we just go through the motions of admitting this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you were in Sarajevo into December of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after 1992, did you return to the city of Sarajevo in subsequent years?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I never stayed there for the same length of time that I had in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And which years were those?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I came -- I went to Sarajevo in 1993 and 1994 and 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And on those visits to Sarajevo, did you continue to send SkyNews reports about the events in that city?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did. Not always that I was immediately sending a report, but I -- yes, I was still reporting for SkyNews as a full-time staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can please go back to 1991 where you mention you had been reporting from Croatia about the conflict there. Did you ever make any television reports about a man known as Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Captain Dragan is an Australian-Serb, Serb-Australian, who came back to Yugoslavia in the early '90s. I don't know the precise date when he came back. I encountered him in July 1991 for the first time in a town called Dvor Na Uni. He took me to a town called Glina that he said that he had just captured with his militia, a militia that was based in the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the reports -- were the reports that you did about Captain Dragan broadcast on SkyNews?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have the full name of this Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name that I have is Captain Dragan, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During your reporting of the events in Croatia, did anyone in the Yugoslav Army at that time make any comments to you about your reports?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: On return to Belgrade at the end of July, having spent ten days or so with Serb forces in Krajina and Banja areas of Croatia, we had a meeting with one of the officers dealing with the press at the Yugoslav Ministry of Defence within Belgrade, and he was certainly aware of the reports that we had sent, yes. Later in the autumn we met other officers who were also aware of the reporting that we had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you tell us about a particular officer or person who indicated that he or she was aware of your reports?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Apart from the officer running the press office, whose name I do not recall, the other person that I absolutely remember talking to me about the reports that I had done was General Kadijevic, at that time the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army and, as I recall, the Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you became aware that persons in Serbia were watching your broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. Other people would comment on the reports that we had done. As I mentioned on Friday, our reports were shown on the third channel of the Belgrade Television, and people would say that they had seen them and make comments about them of various natures, either that they were impressed or less impressed, of whatever nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the persons who were less impressed by your SkyNews reports, how did they express themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to object on a number of grounds, not the least of which is relevance. And who are these persons? What world are we in? We're fighting ghosts now. The persons who were less impressed. You can't be vaguer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this evidence goes to the issue of notice, the fact that persons in Belgrade spoke to this person, even persons who he did not know their identity of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That may well be the case, Your Honour, but what they had to say, those persons who were less impressed, does not go to the issue of notice; it goes to the issue of what their personal opinions may be, whatever those opinions may be. The issue of notice is relatively clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It goes to the -- well, the Prosecution believes this evidence would indicate that people had been watching the reports of Mr. van Lynden, Your Honour. That is the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, Mr. Saxon, the very fact that these people do say to Mr. van Lynden, We did see footage of your reports, whether or not they express an opinion on those reports, that does show that they have seen the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is the Prosecution's position, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So, indeed, it is not up -- it is not necessary for purposes of notice to know what the opinion was of the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you permitted to remain in Serbia, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was permitted to remain in Serbia until April 1994 when my accreditation, which was full time, was revoked by the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were you told why your accreditation had been revoked?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were sent -- the SkyNews office in Belgrade where I was at that time was sent a fax on Friday afternoon informing us that my accreditation had been revoked, with one of the reasons -- and I cannot remember the precise terminology, but that my work had not been in favour of the peaceful -- the peaceful living-together of different peoples, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness 65 ter 532, please, or the first page of it, if I can say that. Your Honours, 65 ter 532 is a tape-recording of the 50th Session of the National Assembly of the Republika Srpska held on the 15th and 16th of April, 1995, in Sanski Most. I should say it is a transcript of a tape-recording. And we see the first page here in both languages. Can we move, please, to, in the English version, page 250, and in the B/C/S version, page 216.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. van Lynden, if you're following me here on page 250 of the English version and 216 of the B/C/S version, we see in the English version -- a bit more than halfway down the page, we see the name "Mr. Toholj", T-O-H-O-L-J, taking the floor. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn now to page 252 in the English version and page 218 in e-court. In the English version. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. van Lynden, in the first full paragraph, the penultimate sentence reads the following: "I also know what happened to the famous journalist, the famous Serb-hater, Van Linder (?) of SkyNews, how he managed to get to Bihac. He stayed there for seven days, and I think that his reporting was prejudicial for our offensive on Bihac." Was there anyone else in the SkyNews team in the former Yugoslavia at that time with the name -- with a last name similar to yours?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Had you received or heard similar descriptions of you in the past?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As a famous journalist and as a famous Serb-hater? Famous journalist, not always, but certain people felt and had made it clear that they thought that I was prejudiced against the Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would seek to tender the pages of this 65 ter exhibit that we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would only ask that they be marked for identification at this point in time based upon further inquiry that may be had with regard to the authentication of this particular document. I don't think it's ultimately going to be a problem, but just for purposes at this particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the document is deemed relevant and has probative value, the Prosecution submits it should be admitted now. If Mr. Guy-Smith in the future finds material that indicates this is not an authentic document, he can certainly raise that and revisit this issue with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the document will be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after 1995 in other parts of Yugoslavia, did you receive, shall I say, derogatory descriptions about your work?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In 1999, just before the NATO attacks --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object on the grounds of relevance as to whether he received other derogatory descriptions about his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, this goes to the fact of notice and the issue of how widespread Mr. van Lynden's reports were seen and watched in the former Yugoslavia, even into 19 -- well, and even in other parts of the former Yugoslavia. That is the relevance to notice, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, indeed, his answer is in 1999, which is well outside of the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It goes to the scope of the notice that was available to this accused, Your Honour, how widely this man's reports were disseminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I understand the Prosecution's argument, there are no -- there are no particular temporal bounds to the notice with regard to Mr. Perisic. This is so far outside of the indictment period that it verges on being laughable with regard to this particular argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not a matter of temporal bounds. It's geographic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With respect to temporal bounds, I would imagine that there is also some submission from the Prosecution that the duty to punish extended far beyond the temporal boundaries of the indictment. If my memory serves me well, that's what Mr. Harmon said in his opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour, as a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And on that basis, then, I would allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, once again, the answer is -- what he's discussing here, the witness' answer deals with 1999. By 1999, Mr. Perisic is no longer the Chief of Staff; Mr. Perisic is no longer in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. But we're dealing here with the question of notice, is it -- it's just the question of notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After 19 -- well, I'll let you begin. You were referring to 1999. Can you briefly describe what happened to you in 1999.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was allowed by the government of Montenegro to enter Montenegro, and I spent a month in Montenegro, and that was during the first month of the NATO attacks on Serbia and Montenegro that then formed Yugoslavia because of the situation in Kosovo. During that time, I was given protection by the police of President Djukanovic that was really attacked on a daily basis out on the streets, both in Podgorica and in other places within Montenegro that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall anything specifically that was said in reference to you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That they felt that I was against the Serbs and that my reports were prejudiced against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever interview Radovan Karadzic for SkyNews?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I didn't so much interview him formally, but I had a lot of conversations. There were two television -- televised interviews, but the rest were conversations with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall approximately when those television interviews took place?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In 1992 and in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it difficult to convince Mr. Karadzic to be interviewed by SkyNews on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. Mr. Karadzic was absolutely willing to be interviewed by SkyNews. SkyNews did a lot of interviews with Mr. Karadzic, also, over a telephone line, simply giving him a chance to respond to whatever the latest developments within the war in Bosnia were. And when I returned to Pale in February 1994 following the first market bomb in Sarajevo, Mr. Karadzic, while making it clear that he was not pleased to see me, still gave me an interview and allowed me access and also invited me, as I mentioned earlier, to this one meeting of the political and military leadership of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe my time is about to expire, and at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Any cross-examination, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A question or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sir, you come from an old titled family in Europe. Your grandfather or great grandfather, if I'm not mistaken, was a military man of some measure. If you were to describe yourself as a wine, you would call yourself "a hedonistic St. Emilion, of course." You prefer not to be called by the name of Baron, if I'm not mistaken, so I will call you Mr. van Lynden, with your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Van Lynden will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't quite get -- I would call myself a what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A hedonistic St. Emilion.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring, of course, to your slight coup with your Le Tetra Roteboeuf 1990 because you're a wine collector, also, I understand.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Of a small nature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to understand, if I could, your military service. Your military service, as you related to us, was national service, and if I'm not mistaken, is the same two -year, I will call it, stint that all young men in the Netherlands had to perform during that period of time before the national service was no longer compulsory, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the Netherlands, the standard procedure was that anyone doing national service would have to do 14 months in the armed forces. Instead, I chose to apply to do my national service with the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps. That entailed doing a one-year officer training and then serving minimally for a year as a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And that is precisely what you did.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then after two years of military service, you stopped serving in the National Marine Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I became part of the National Marine Reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in your capacity as a National Marine Reserve, were you called to duty at any point in time, or did you periodically go on annual operations?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was called up once for one of these operations. They were not annual, usually, in nature, but at that time I had left the Netherlands already and was actually in Pakistan and about to enter Afghanistan with the Afghan resistance during the war with the Soviet Union in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it would have been a bit difficult for you to return, I take it.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I only actually heard about it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Now, during your time as a war reporter, you had been, as I understand your testimony, in a number of conflicts throughout the world, correct? THE COURT REPORTER: I am having difficulty hearing Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The court reporter says that they're having difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the dropped voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said during your time as a war reporter, you have been involved in a number of conflicts, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I haven't been involved with them. I've covered them, yes, but I'm specifically in the Middle East. That was my main area where I worked as a war correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a war correspondent, there are a couple of considerations -- I'm sure there are myriad considerations, but a couple of considerations that always come to the fore, one of them certainly being access to the fighting units.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. In covering a war one needs to try to get access to the front lines to be able to form an impression --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- and to report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in terms of reporting, that's to accurately and objectively report that which is going on during any particular battle or, for that matter, a cease-fire or any other operation that you see.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, getting access to front lines is of importance for war correspondents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the specific conflict that we're interested in here, obviously before you went to the region, you educated yourself with regard to who the players were, did you not, who were the individuals of importance?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, to a degree, and that education continued as we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sure it did. Now, when you first arrived in Sarajevo, so we're clear, the military forces that were engaged at that time included the ABiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, which was still a force, though, under construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say it was a force under construction, I take it that you mean by that that it was not an army proper yet and that, indeed, during the time that you were there - and by that I mean at the very beginning - there was also a Territorial Defence, militias of various individuals who you referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very sorry to interrupt, but perhaps if we could simply have one question at a time to make it easier for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was also a group of individuals who were the Territorial Defence who were distinct from the ABiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's how I recall it from May 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in addition to the ABiH and the Territorial Defence, there were also various militia groups.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they referred to themselves as militia groups, but I certainly encountered one unit led by a man called Jusuf Prazina. Whether we would call it a militia or not, he seemed very much in control himself of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, to fairly characterise, for example, the group that you've just mentioned, there were -- in addition to the Territorial Defence and the ABiH, there were groups of armed individuals who were working together against the JNA; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And on the -- have I taken into account now all of the groups, military groups, that were on, let's say, one side of the conflict? Have I missed anyone?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And on the other side of that conflict was the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from the JNA, were there any other military groups on the other side of that conflict? When you first got there. When you first got there.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But in 1992 you're referring to, in Bosnia, not 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were armed militia of a man known as Arkan, Zeljko Raznjatovic, known as Arkan's Tigers, whom I encountered in the field, and I also met Arkan in Belgrade, and there were armed groups led by a man called Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the complexion of things changed in 1992, and by that I mean the gentleman who you have characterised as the scourge of Sarajevo became the commander of an army, right?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, he was already a commander in the army. He was in Knin in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In May of 1992, he became the commander of the VRS, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware. I wasn't there at the -- I mean, I wasn't with him at the time of his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, but you certainly were aware of the fact that in May of 1992 he was designated and appointed by the government the commander of the VRS, correct? That being Mr. Karadzic's --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's government. And he was responsible to Mr. Karadzic, who I take it - and do correct me if I'm wrong - was the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember him ever referring to himself as the Supreme Commander Of Republika Srpska. I mean, he was the political leader and as far as I recall, Mr. Mladic was the military leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was he Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska, or was he the Supreme Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: An excellent question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said, an excellent question, Your Honour, which I will ask, having His Honour's question in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Mr. Karadzic the Supreme Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska or, if you know, the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska? If you know. If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was the President of the Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- which at that stage wasn't called the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, there came a time when some troops - and I believe this was in May - of the JNA while leaving Sarajevo were ambushed. Are you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware of the incident. It happened before I entered Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Those troops, the troops that were ambushed, they were ambushed by, if you know, the ABiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I wasn't there, and I have heard various versions of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that you heard various versions of that incident, what you have heard is that either the ABiH or the militia groups or citizen groups were involved in the ambush of those troops as they were leaving pursuant to an agreement to leave, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware that they were fired on, but I'm -- I don't know who did the firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how many were killed?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when I say "JNA," those would be young Serbian boys who were soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not necessarily only Serbian. I encountered in Sarajevo in the former military hospital, the reason I first went there, as I recall, the man who was being cared for was someone doing his national service who was actually from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely. So in the ambush that occurred, there were young boys from many ethnicities or certainly from more than one ethnicity who were ambushed by forces in opposition to the JNA. That would be, I think, a fair way of putting it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, I don't know who was actually hitting this, but I'm aware in the JNA that there were people from more than just Serbia and Montenegro still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the Marsal Tito barracks, the barracks which we saw a video-clip about, the Marsal Tito barracks were barracks that were under the dominion and control of the JNA until they departed from Sarajevo, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if my memory serves with regard to the testimony you've given to us in that regard, those barracks had within them, apart from human beings, they also had military ordinance of some sort and fashion that was left behind, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, yes, but I didn't get inside those barracks after their evacuation, so I wasn't able to see with my own eyes what was or was not left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports as to -- from any of the myriad sources that you had with regard to what was left behind?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What we were told was that there was ammunition that had been left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in your experience as a soldier as well as in your experience as a war correspondent, it would not be prudent to leave ammunition behind for the use of your opponent, now, would it? That would not be militarily a wise thing to do.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not particularly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And once having evacuated a particular area, for example, a barracks or a compound where such ammunition was, it would be militarily prudent to destroy it, to blow it up, to get rid of it so that your opponent would not have access to that particular ammunition, correct? That would be a prudent thing to do.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From a military standpoint, yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to -- with regard to the issue of the ABiH, the Territorial Defence and the militia, would it be fair to say that there was a standing - and you may not like that particular term "standing" - but there was a standing armed force of an excess of 80.000 soldiers in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have never heard the precise numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you have heard -- you've heard numbers.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Oh. I mean, no, at that stage it was completely unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Bigger --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Totally unclear, and I suspect it would be unclear to the actual people who were saying that they were in command at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have an expression "bigger than a bread basket," which is a bit off point. But there were a fair number of individual soldiers who were fighting first against the JNA and then certainly against Mr. -- General Mladic, weren't there? And by "fair number," I'm saying it numbered within the thousands, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tens of thousands? And I'm not -- once again, I'm not trying to pin you down to any particular number because, as you said, it was unclear. There was a formidable group of fighting men.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What period are we talking about? What time spent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But 1992 and 1991, there was absolutely not Bosnian army --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. 1992. I do apologise. 1992.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: And in 1992, it developed. It was a changing situation. By the end of the year, you had a Bosnian army that was in control, and a Jukef -- a Jusuf Prazina who was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was an evolving situation, and their numbers may have changed over that time and of those who had been called up and then trained. And those were not figures that we were ever actually given by the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say it was a revolving army, that's not dissimilar to what occurred, for example, in Kosovo. There was a revolving army in Kosovo starting in the beginning of 1998, the KLA, and then certainly by September, October, it was a much different force than when it began.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I wasn't in Kosovo, and I would not compare what occurred there with what occurred in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Nor compare the Bosnian army to the KLA. I do not think they are comparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm only dealing from a standpoint of an evolving army, no more than that, nothing more than just a revolving army.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I would refer to the KLA as an army. In Bosnia, an army did evolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there's been much dispute as to whether or not there was an army in the KLA, and there are those that think that there wasn't and those that think that there was. With regard to the issue of snipers, there were snipers in Sarajevo in 1992 who operated on both sides of the conflict, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity during the time that you were engaged in your reportage to meet with the snipers who were part of the ABiH or any of the other groups that were there?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to just explain something. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we continue now? You may. You may continue, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To give you a full answer, I have to explain that as a war correspondent you don't go out with a sniper if you use your brain beforehand. I have encountered snipers but never at my own request. This comes from an early experience in Beirut when I was very young still, and an American journalist who had not thought it through went out with a Lebanese sniper because he wanted to do a story about the day in the life of a sniper. And when they arrived at the allotted point, the sniper turned to the journalist and said, Okay, there are two people in my sights. Whom would you like me to kill? Which put the journalist in an impossible ethical position, as I'm sure Your Honour will understand. And I have never throughout my career, therefore, asked to spend a day in the life of a sniper. The only sniping snipers that I encountered were not at my request. I asked to go to the front lines. But I encountered a couple of snipers on the Serb -- Bosnian Serb side in September 1992 in Grbavica. On the Bosnian side, I was never with a sniper or with a sniping unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the explanation, but just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the front line, and so we're clear, would it be fair to say that the city of Sarajevo itself in 1992, when you were -- when you were - thank you, Mr. Mair - when you were engaged in your reporting was populated with Bosnian military who were fighting?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The city was populated by the population of Sarajevo. Amongst them were military who were fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those military that were fighting in the city that was populated were, as you've told us, in the tens of thousands, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I didn't say tens of thousands. I don't know the numbers. But there were certainly thousands of armed men. But I should add that most of them were on the front lines. It was a very long front line in Sarajevo. And if I look back at the period in 1992, as well as my memory serves me, I do not remember encountering a lot of military men walking around in the city centre. Where you saw them were out on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you were reporting, the actual reporting that you did, and by that I mean is, was it a videotape? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know what -- you know, what system you were using. The videotape was transported to the offices at Belgrade 3 for some period of time.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please explain -- just explain to us the mechanics of where the ultimate programme was compiled. Was that done in London, or was that done in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My report --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- was -- in 1991, it was usually done in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But sometimes in -- for instance, in the early part, well, I mean July, we had a base in Bihac and we compiled the report there. In Bosnia, there was a period in May/June 1992 when the editor, the person -- the picture editor was in Pale and I was in Sarajevo. I would write the report, but the pictures that were put over it were put over it by the picture editor in Pale. In later periods, later June, July, August, September, and October, November, December, all those reports were compiled by me either in Pale but with me and the picture editor, for instance, those in September, and those later in the year with me with the picture editor in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say -- when you say "with the picture editor," just so we're clear, what happened out on the ground was that you and your crew took footage --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with that -- you then examined that footage at a later point in time, later that day, and made a determination what part of that footage would be appropriate for a report. And I'm saying that in a value-neutral sense.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's the way television works.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the way television works.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The usual is that you film -- have about half an hour on film, and you use one minute in an actual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. It's about a 1:30 shooting range.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Something like that. Now, the scripting that was done is the -- and I mean no disrespect when I say this, the scripting that was done is the creative writing component of your reportage. You make a determination of what words to use. You make a determination of how many adjectives to use, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Absolutely. And that's done by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's all done by you.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The script, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in the reporting that you did, you made a decision with each one of those reports, whether or not you were working with the picture editor or -- meaning directly or whether or not you sent to the picture editor your script, you made a determination in each one of those reportings as to the emotional impact, apart from obviously the reporting, the emotional impact that you intended for your report to have, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. That's not really what you're doing. You're trying to tell the story as clearly as possible for the audience as to what you saw, what you filmed, and what you think -- you believe happened. It's not about getting an emotional impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's just straight objective -- straight objective, This is what happened, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. What we try, but we do not always succeed in -- by "objective," none of us is objective. We cannot be objective. But what we mean and what we try but where we sometimes fail is to leave out personal opinion and to report it as clearly and honestly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm. The agreement that you had - by that I mean SkyNews had - with Belgrade 3 is that the reportage would occur sometime during every day, correct, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, Belgrade, the third channel, put out, as I recall, 12 hours a day, and those were 12 consecutive hours, or maybe it had been split up. That, I can't precisely recall. But as I remember, it was that they were broadcasting SkyNews for 12 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know -- as you said, you can't remember, so you couldn't tell us whether that was during the daytime or in the early morning hours after midnight?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I can't precisely recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us with regard to the transmissions from Belgrade during that period of time whether those transmissions were in any language other than English, the SkyNews transmissions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: SkyNews was only broadcast in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether or not the transmissions, pursuant to this agreement you had, had, as we saw, for example, here in court --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Were subtitled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Subtitle -- thank you, subtitles in the B/C/S. Can you tell us that? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, they were never subtitled, and the language at that stage was still Serbo-Croat, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. And with regard to those transmissions, do you know what the - I'm now moving away from the temporal issue to a geographic issue - do you know what the distance was of the transmissions from Belgrade 3 during this period of time? And by "distance," I mean a kilometre distance. How far from Belgrade proper did these transmissions emanate, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether it was only in central Belgrade. We were -- we were told that it was viewable in Belgrade but not in the whole of Serbia, but I don't -- I simply don't know. That's really up to the -- I mean, that was a technical --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's technical stuff.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's not our television station so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just to -- because we're dealing for a moment in some technical stuff, as you sit here today, you can't really tell us, apart from the fact that you know it was broadcast in Belgrade, whether or not it was picked up anywhere else in the country.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we were certainly aware that it was picked up both in Zagreb and in Sarajevo, SkyNews, and that in both countries they produced programmes, something with titles like, What others are saying about us. I think the programme was in Zagreb. I don't recall the precise title. But those were evening programmes which were a compilation of what SkyNews, CNN, BBC, had broadcast that day about the conflict in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to just touch on one more point, which is you mentioned that in your experience, if I heard your testimony correctly, that western armies in Iraq and Iran - and maybe I misheard you - but that western armies do not use incendiary rounds. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What I'm aware is that NATO armies do not have incendiary rounds fired from rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's distinct from, I think, what you said. You said "western armies," which is why I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But what I meant was NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: NATO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: So American and British specifically, and the Dutch. And I'm talking about incendiary rounds fired from rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, so -- so they do have incendiary rounds.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't know if they have incendiary rounds from artillery. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- apart from white phosphorus, which they do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But not from rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They have -- so they do have white phosphorus, which is an incendiary round if they --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's a mortar round.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Or artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And western armies use that particular incendiary round throughout the world in their conflicts, don't they?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do not know whether they are using it at the moment still, but they certainly were using it when I was in the Dutch Marine Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And they certainly were using it in Afghanistan, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of -- I haven't been in Afghanistan over the last seven years. I don't know if it's used in Afghanistan or not. It was used by the Soviet Union in Afghanistan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm talking about now just the western armies.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I haven't covered Afghanistan since that conflict -- the new conflict came up in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your covering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you when it might be convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it's convenient for me now. I'm sorry. I haven't gotten my -- I haven't gotten my internal clock put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. It's the first time you're standing up in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But the other thing is that we may not have very many --any questions left for the witness, so I don't know how the Chamber wishes to handle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About how many more minutes do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have 15 seconds with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't mean to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. No, you didn't. No, please. Please, I was getting very close to my end in any event. We're fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just want to know if I can get a bottle of the wine. He apparently has a slamming wine, Your Honour, which I'd really like to get a bottle of, but I mean, that's probably a different issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've sold it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely. Okay. Could we take a break now and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, during your cross-examination you mentioned that General Mladic was already a commander in Knin in 1991. This is at page 25 of the LiveNote for today. Just to clarify, of which army was Mr. Mladic a commander in 1991?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was a JNA corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Also, in your testimony you were asked by my learned colleague whether the SkyNews broadcasts or reports that were received in Belgrade, were they only broadcast -- were they broadcast in English and you responded, no, they were not, nor they were -- nor were they broadcast in Serbo -- I apologise, because I've gotten my languages mixed up. You testified that these reports were broadcast only in English, correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The broadcasts were only in English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there were no Serbo-Croat subtitles attached to these reports.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: None, unless the reports were shown, as I also mentioned, on Croatian or Bosnian television when they may have had subtitles. That, I can't recall, but certainly not as I recall on the third channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you were in Belgrade, did anyone ever try to speak to you in the English language about one or more of your reports or say anything to you about them?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe one or two examples?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Various people, people from within journalism but also someone like Zeljko Raznjatovic who actually called me in 1993 when I was in Brussels and spoke to me in English about the reporting that I had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is the man also known as Arkan?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You have testified on cross-examination, you had clarified that NATO armies do not have incendiary rounds for rifles; and in the last video-clip that I showed you today, we saw some incendiary rounds striking a building. Were you able to ascertain or observe whether those were incendiary rounds for rifles or not?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That was rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify. The Trial Chamber wants to say a special thanks to you for taking the time off from your busy schedule to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague, Ms. Edgerton, will lead the next witness. Your Honour, just as a point of scheduling, and I've explained this to Mr. Blumenstock, as well, quite frankly the Prosecution thought that the cross-examination of the last witness would have lasted much longer. We have a single 92 ter witness prepared to testify today, and we have one more 92 ter witness who will be prepared to testify tomorrow. So we will not be able to fill tomorrow, nor will we be able to fill Wednesday or Thursday. We have one witness who we were able to bring here who will be available on Wednesday and one on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks for the update, Mr. Saxon. Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your indulgence for just a few moments while we switch stations, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do that before the witness comes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Prosecution counsel is strongly urged to use a long microphone instead of the short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, you are not wearing your earphones. The interpreters ask that you use the long microphone instead of the short one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. I was listening to the French channel inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. I realise you were not wearing one, and I thought I must just make you aware of what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm all ears now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You wanted to say something, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I thought that my colleague, the Prosecutor, would address the Trial Chamber in view of the procedural problem that we are facing now, we the Defence, through no fault of our own. During the break between our two sessions, I received proofing notes from the OTP for this witness consisting of seven points in the English language, and I've been informed by the OTP that at 2.45 they had sent this to our web mail in B/C/S. At any rate, I believe that this is the last time that we communicate in this way with regard to proofing notes. I really never had experience like this, that I get the proofing notes at the moment when the witness is walking into the courtroom. I've already consulted the Prosecutor, and they said that they would agree. Obviously, in terms of time we will be able to deal with this witness, so could I please be given a half-hour break to consult my client and to consult with Mr. Guy-Smith with regard to these proofing notes because, really, we have been taken aback by all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to stand down right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that would be the most appropriate way of dealing with it. We should not start with the witness before we've been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, can we make sure that next time we give the proofing notes timely so that we save on court time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course, in as much as possible. The only delay in producing these today was that they were done late last night in English, and I wanted to have a Bosnian language translation prepared so that the witness could read the material in her own language. There was delay in getting the translation. Then, of course, it was brought to the witness at her hotel, so certainly no lack of attentiveness to the matter. But in as much as possible, we'll endeavour to produce these in as timely a fashion as possible. My apologies for the delay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You want 30 minutes? Do you want us to come back at 20 to? Okay. We'll take a short adjournment and come back at 20 to 5.00. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 4.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
