utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have to point out our concern with regard to the situation that we're in right now. The witness who is supposed to walk into the courtroom today was called as a 92 ter witness, and we are fully aware of the situation that the Prosecution is facing with regard to the order of witnesses and everything that had been happening over the past few days. All of it is not in line with the procedure that is supposed to be there in terms of receiving 92 ter material and possibly objecting to it. However, what we received right now, the proofing notes, is far beyond the summary that the OTP provided in their pre-trial brief. On the 1st of March, 2007, the OTP put this witness on their list and clearly stated what the reason was, why they're calling that witness. You do have that, Your Honours. It has to do with the incident that the witness already testified about and the incident that is described in the witness statement. In the proofing notes we've just received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please be seated, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not used to having two counsel standing at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The proofing notes that we've received just now contain a description of other incidents, new ones altogether, two out of which have never been mentioned before, whereas the remaining four, or rather, three incidents that are mentioned - there's a total of five - have to do with a broader explanation of the things that she already testified about in the Dragomir Milosevic case. This concerns something that is clearly stated in the decision of the Pre-Trial Judge from 2007, what we discussed the other day, that is. If the OTP wants to question a witness in relation to unscheduled incidents, then they have to notify the Defence four weeks in advance. These are completely new incidents. Some of them are outside the time of the indictment, and as for others we don't even know when it was that they happened. I believe that the Pre-Trial Chamber, when passing this decision on four weeks, believed that the Defence should use that time either to object in order to have the OTP state a good reason why the incidents should be discussed in court and for the Defence to be able to check what the OTP says. However, we are in a position not to be able to investigate certain incidents, and now we are supposed to hear the witness about that, and we've just been informed about all of this before the witness walks into the courtroom. I have to mention another thing that I find even more perplexing, and the Prosecutor can confirm that for me. This witness was first interviewed by the OTP in 1995 about what happened in Sarajevo. Her second statement was made in 2006, again, to the OTP. Then she testified in the Milosevic case in February 2007, and before that proofing notes were compiled by the OTP, always in relation to what it was that had happened in Sarajevo. So there were three meetings with the OTP, and the first one took place more than ten years ago, and from all of that we received nothing from the OTP. So we really cannot cross-examine the witness about things that we first hear of here in the courtroom today. And in relation to the summary provided by the OTP, these incidents only have to do with what it is that she is going to testify about. So we propose that the Prosecutor not be allowed to carry out a direct examination about anything else but the original incidents; otherwise, we will have to call the same witness again within four weeks, or rather, four weeks later, and in the meantime the Prosecutor should provide good reasons for why they want to discuss other incidents in court with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, which are the incidents that are new?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the Prosecutor has copies of the proofing notes they gave us, but the first incident is the one that happened immediately after the other incident that has to do with shooting at the tram, as stated in the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Give us the incident number. I guess you said they were in the proofing notes. You just said -- which paragraphs are these that are new?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you have also received the proofing notes, then I believe incidents from paragraphs 1 and 2 are new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then paragraph 4 and paragraph 3, as well, although there is some mention of that in the Milosevic case. You know what? Had we received this four weeks ago, as we were supposed to receive in keeping with 92 ter, we could have stated our views with regard to this statement. I understand now that timing is difficult for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we haven't got much time. Okay. I'm not quite sure I understand why you say number 3 is also new when it has been testified to in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a clarification, but it is an incident from 1992, and now all of a sudden there is this broader explanation provided here. This is a description of events that is not what is contained in the summary. If you look at the summary, what the Prosecutor said in the summary, it only had to do with this incident; and in the last paragraph she speaks of her walk along the street as she was going to the university. This incident is not included in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, do you have any response to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, on just a couple of points. The Prosecution's submission is that the incidents in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 are not new incidents at all and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Let me interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The paragraphs that are alleged to be new are 1, 2, 3, and 4, not 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies, Your Honour. 3 and 4 are not new incidents at all, and in fact the text of the paragraph specifically refers to the page number of the previous testimony of Mrs. Mulaosmanovic in respect of these incidents. This is mere clarification of the events that she testified to earlier, which is often the purpose of proofing. And the information that's recorded here, I would submit, Your Honour, really serves quite well to put the Defence on notice, in fact, to make his job easier when he chooses to engage in cross-examination. But my friend raised another point, Your Honour, that I'd actually prefer to address Your Honours on, and that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'd prefer you to address me on what he alleges. 1 and 2 look new to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you address me on those -- address us on those, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. They are. And I learned of these incidents in proofing when the witness mentioned, "That wasn't the only time I was shot at on a tram," and of course, I recorded those and gave that information to the witness to confirm in her own language as soon as I was able to; and once that information was confirmed, we passed it to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but do you understand the gravamen of the objection? The gravamen of the objection is that they should have received that kind of information some four weeks earlier. Now, given the fact that you're telling them about these new incidents for the first time today, they want to reserve the right to recall the witness sometime in the future for cross-examination on those two items. And to avoid that, they are suggesting that -- they are submitting, in fact, that you not be allowed to lead the witness on those two points. They say four, but you say the other two come from previous proceedings. But at least there are these two that you also concede are new.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I would like you to address their submission or their prayer that you not be allowed to lead on those that are new.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment to check the transcript, Your Honour. I think my friend raised a couple of points with respect to that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He did. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There were two points as I can see it, Your Honours, and the first refers to the Rule 73 bis decision of 2007, and the second has to do -- has to do with timeliness of the notice, and I'd like to address Your Honours on both of those points, if I may. With respect to the first, I think it really puts us in a position where we need to, with respect, evaluate or assess the scope, the intention behind that 73 bis ruling. The type of evidence that this witness spoke about and was provided in the proofing note isn't, I would submit, Your Honours, detailed, forensic examination of an incident that might rise to the level of a scheduled incident, one that we might call police officers for, forensic technicians for, and other victim evidence. This is, I would submit, Your Honour, much more a question of -- evidence of general conditions around the time of the incident or general conditions that the witness was living in Sarajevo between 1994 and 1995. I don't think, Your Honour, that 73 bis ruling was contemplating a detailed forensic examination. There are some particular unscheduled incidents that, indeed, I think the Prosecution would be filing a motion on four weeks in advance; those, for example, where we might seek to call evidence of unscheduled incidents through police officers, the situation generally, and evidence about the manufacture of the shells in particular. There are those where I think we might seek to call evidence of unscheduled incidents and the situation generally, again, through people who have the expertise. But this is just additional evidence, Your Honour, from a young woman talking about what was it like to live in the conditions that civilians in the centre of Sarajevo had in 1994 and 1995. I would suggest, Your Honour, this is evidence that goes to widespread and systematic and actually isn't, Your Honours, caught by the 73 bis decision. With respect to the timeliness, Your Honour, and I've made it quite clear; I've endeavoured to provide the most accurate piece of information to Defence counsel that I could in the time given. I have said already that the reason it took so long to deliver that information to Defence counsel is that I needed to have -- I felt it best to have the witness confirm that information in her own language. I think we're all working with a little bit of difficulty in the circumstances of the case this week and the short notice within which the witnesses were called. But given the type of incident we're talking about, the fact that she's testified three times, the nature of the additional information that's not really going to the gravamen of the offence, as I've said, I would submit that my friends have had more than sufficient notice and an extra half an hour to see whether or not they might want to expand on that information in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My friend's on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please allow your friend to finish, unless you have an objection to raise, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we are talking too much now about things that are pertaining to procedure, but we are at the very beginning of the trial so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, unless you're having an objection, I'm asking you to please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I had believed that she had finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, are you done?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was about to conclude with the final request, Your Honour, that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do. Please do conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- that should we decide to lead this evidence, there's no prejudice suffered to the Defence in any regard, and it's not the type of information that should be excluded as an unscheduled incident by virtue of the 73 bis ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're at the very beginning of the trial now, and now we are setting the rules, as it were, especially in relation to 92 ter procedure. The understanding of my learned friend is such that I'm afraid that we are going to move into viva voce testimony. If so, I don't mind changing the status of the witness; however, we have to receive notification of that in good time. I believe that the Prosecutor is now trying to bring in through the back door things that are not contained in 92 ter witnesses. We have prepared for 92 ter witnesses. There are going to be other witnesses who are going to be viva voce; however, the Prosecutor called this witness with regard to particular incidents. That's what the summary says, and that is the basic idea of bringing people in to testify in accordance with Rule 92 ter. If they want to call a witness to speak about other aspects of their lives, then this has to be a viva voce witness. I believe that this kind of precedent would create great problems for us in the future, if through the proofing notes we find out about new facts only a day or two before we actually hear the witness. Regardless of whether the witness is saying this through an additional statement or by way of clarification of the previous statement made, all of these are new facts for us; and the summary of this witness clearly states why she was called in the first place. I'm sure that the Prosecutor will be able to prove their case, the Prosecution case, in different ways; but that was not what they intended, obviously, on the basis of the summary of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's going to give its ruling. The Prosecution is not allowed to canvas items 1 and 2 of the proofing note. It may canvas the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, given that this witness's testimony is as a 92 ter witness and in accordance with discussions that the parties were involved in, we've prepared a short summary of the evidence of this witness that we'd like to read into the record, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. The greater part of this witness' evidence, Your Honours, is going to be in respect of scheduled sniping incident 10 of the indictment against General Perisic; and as a 92 ter witness, Mrs. Mulaosmanovic has previously given evidence in proceedings in this Tribunal in the case of the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, and she'll confirm that evidence today. In summary, her evidence is that she was born and raised in Sarajevo, and on 27 February 1995 she was an 18-year-old economics student in her home town. Around midday on that date, she boarded a crowded tram near the cathedral. The tram was heading from Bascarsija towards Cengic Vila in the west. It was filled with men, women, and children, all civilians. As the tram passed in the open area of the crossroads between the Earth Museum and the Museum of Revolution, the witness stood facing the former Marsal Tito barracks. She heard a burst of fire from behind her, from what she described as the neighbourhoods of Grbavica and Vraca. People crouched for cover. The fire continued and the tram was hit, wounding Mrs. Mulaosmanovic in her left arm. Mrs. Mulaosmanovic gave evidence as to the location she believed was the origin of fire, illustrated with maps and photographs, which she marked in court. The witness did not recall any military vehicles, seeing any combat activity, or any Bosnian army soldiers near the tram at the time of the incident. The shooting continued until the tram moved to a sheltered location and stopped. The witness was taken for emergency medical care, treated, and sent home. Mrs. Mulaosmanovic gave evidence that during 1994 and 1995 there was intense sniping in Sarajevo. She noted that throughout the war, whether you were moving about or sitting in your home, you could hear shells and gunfire. Nowhere in town was safe, even inside one's flat. You never knew when they were going to land. She described the fear and suspense of not knowing whether you may be shot or injured and the sense of relief when the projectiles passed by. That's the summary of the witness' evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we now going to have counsel testify and then the witness testify before -- and this is a 92 ter witness? I found your summary so long that it seemed to cover the entire statement that -- testimony of this witness as contained in her statement. Now, you're going to ask her questions again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask her to introduce herself and ask whether she had reviewed her statements and previous testimony and associated exhibits and offer them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's what I was going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you state your name.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Alma Mulaosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were you born Alma Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, prior to you appearing here today, did you have occasion to review a statement you gave to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you review it in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you have any additions, deletions, or alterations to make to that statement?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was just one correction concerning a last name, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall that correction?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Cehajic" was misspelled with a "G" instead of a "J."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's a correction you made during your previous testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case. Perhaps we could move on. Now, also before coming to court today, did you review a further statement you gave to the OTP in 2006?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was also in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And other than a typographical error that you noticed on the front cover sheet in terms of the date of the interview, do you have any other additions, deletions, or alterations to make to that statement?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you have a pretty good command of English, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, then, before testifying here today, did you also review an English-language copy of your testimony in cross-examination before this Tribunal in the Dragomir Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you understood everything you read?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you also review copies of maps, photographs, and documents which were dealt with in your testimony during that trial?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In respect of all this previously given evidence, if you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honours, could I list by 65 ter number the materials referred to in the 92 ter package and ask that they be marked as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give the 65 ter number, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. The first one is 09249, which is the 1996 statement; 09250, which is the 2006 statement; 09255, which is the transcript of the previously given evidence with those portions the Prosecution is relying upon highlighted; 09251, which is a marked map; 09252, a marked photo; 09253, another marked photo; and 02708, a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter documents 09249, 09250, 09255, 09251, 09252, 09253, and 02708 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number as a package.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 09249 will become Exhibit P13; 65 ter 09250 will become Exhibit P14; 65 ter 09255 will become Exhibit P15; 65 ter 09251 will become Exhibit P16; 65 ter 09252 will become Exhibit P17; 65 ter 09253 will become Exhibit P18; and 65 ter 02708 will become Exhibit P19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, I have one further document I'd like to put to the witness, and it should take about four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, do you recall whether you were ever interviewed by the police about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you give them a statement?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just ask then, please, e-court 65 ter number 3412, page 21, be pulled up and displayed for Mrs. Mulaosmanovic. 03412, page 21. And page 21 is, of course, the e-court page number. Your Honour, of course my estimate of four minutes was based on technology serving us, and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We should have the B/C/S copy already on the screen. If we could just show that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see, Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it. That's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any additions, deletions, or alterations to that document?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you had read it prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like, please, to tender page -- e-court page 21 of 03412 as the next and last Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We need an English translation into evidence, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The English translation was completed yesterday and is probably in the process of being uploaded, and I am confident it would be available forthwith. If not, of course, we'll be able to provide a hard copy within very short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, because that's the -- that's the version that should be admitted into evidence, and we don't have it here. At least up here, we didn't even see the B/C/S one. I can see it in front of the court officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the B/C/S one on my screen either, Your Honour. That's why I was concerned there was something missing for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, 65 ter 3412 -- I don't know whether you have anything to say, Mr. Lukic. We haven't got the English version here, which is the one that we're supposed to admit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it on my screen either. I see that the witness has it on her screen, but I have a hard copy, so I have no problem. Now we have the B/C/S version on the screen, and we don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the resourceful Ms. Javier has been able to find the English version on e-court and has given some instructions to Madam Usher. It was actually uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then at least we admit into evidence something we see. Can we have the English version on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: She's re-releasing it now, Your Honour, to make sure it becomes available. Your Honour, it was, after all, the first venture into e-court in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Understandable. We were watching maps yesterday, last week. Okay. Then that is the statement. 65 ter 3412, page 21, is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P20, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Mulaosmanovic --

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- during your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic proceedings, at page 1666, you spoke of one of your friends who had died on a balcony which had a concrete wall in front of it. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. It has to do with a girl.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This girl who was killed, do you recall how she died?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was a rather special one. There was no electricity or gas most of the time in houses. It was the month of August. It was summertime. She was cooking lunch on her balcony. A shell fell, and a shrapnel ricochetted somehow and hit her in the head and she got killed on the spot as she was cooking lunch on her balcony that belongs to her own apartment, her home.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In an unfortunate yet similar situation, you referred in your 2006 statement, paragraph 11, to your uncle who died while he was outside of his house. Could you describe how he was killed.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there weren't any furnaces in houses. They were made only later. So he was baking bread in front of the building, in actual fact, and he was also killed by shrapnel from a shell, and his son, who was underage, was with him then. The son was wounded when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember what area of town this took place in?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The second incident was in Dobrinje, in 1992, the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what area of town did the first incident take place in?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: At Cengic Vila, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Edgerton. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have some questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, I am Novak Lukic, and on behalf of the Defence team of General Perisic, I'm going to put a few questions to you, and we will try to deal with this as fast as we can. We know that you came here in quite a hurry, and we will try to deal with all of this as fast as we can.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already had experience in courtrooms, so you know that we speak the same language. Could you please pause before answering my question, and I will also try to pause before putting my following questions so that we do not overlap in the process. Let me clarify something at the very beginning. The first statement in relation to this incident that took place on the 27th of February - that's right, wasn't it - in 1995, that first incident, you made that statement a month or two after that at the police station in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the document does have a date. Yes, that's the first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is 520 [as interpreted] that was just admitted. So on the 14th of April, 1995, you first made a statement in relation to this incident.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you made a statement to the OTP of the Hague Tribunal, and I'm going to call it statement number two, on the 22nd of February, 1996, also in relation to this incident.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then again to the OTP of the Hague Tribunal in March 2006.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then finally after that, you testified here in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt or intervene in your cross-examination, Mr. Lukic, but I just wanted to say that the Chamber does not have what you refer to as the first statement of the 14th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the statement that the Prosecution brought in just now. I'm going to ask the usher to put P20 in e-court. Could we please see both the English and B/C/S versions. Let's just see whether we have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the statement that you gave at the police station in Sarajevo. You will agree with me that at that time your memory was the best in relation to this incident.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this statement you said, and I'm going to quote this statement, it says: "I heard a burst of gunfire from automatic weapons and the thud of bullets in the tram and glass breaking."

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This statement probably faithfully reflected what it was that you said at the police station then, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this statement, you do not mention at all from where you thought the shooting had come, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the statements that you gave after that to the OTP of the Hague Tribunal, again, there is a reference to bursts of gunfire. Can you tell us now: When I read your statement, first of all, you heard some bursts of gunfire in the distance and then, if I understand your statement correctly, then you heard this thud of bullets in the tram, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was this burst of gunfire, and then perhaps a short pause, and then for me the sound was the same of this other burst of gunfire, and then the bullets were hitting the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that the tram was on the move all the time, right? I mean at the moment when you heard the first firing and, also, the other bullets hitting the tram.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a very short difference between the two, if I can put it that way, and the tram was moving all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to go through what it was that you said in the Milosevic case. Let us look at a map so that we all get an impression of this, all of us here in this courtroom. You're our first witness who speaks about certain locations in Sarajevo, and I would like you to indicate for us the location where this incident had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look now at the map. I think it is P15, document P15. I may be mistaken, but we'll see. I've just been informed that it may be 16, P16. Yes, that's it. 09251 is the 65 ter number. I thought I could manage numbers on my own but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, you have already marked certain things on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I don't know whether it would be possible for us to use a different colour to make other markings in court now in order to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we not have a clean map?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't, and I think that this map is pretty useful. At least it was useful to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It could be a map of the same place but clean. That's all I'm asking, and I'm sure it will still be useful, but it's got to be without markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be very useful if the OTP had a map like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you'll just indulge me for another brief second, I think I can tell you what 65 ter number the clean version of this map is. If I can just have a little moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter 4448, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 4448, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, I'm sure it's 65 ter 4448.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're waiting for the map, Mrs. Mulaosmanovic. We have read your statements and your testimony. You often took that route, every day when you went to university and when you went to high school, as all of this was happening in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Often, yes, but not all the time. This was the route that the tram took, but then there was an alternative route that I'd take on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I know is that the tram started operating in Sarajevo sometime in March 1994. Would that be right? Is that your recollection, too?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm sorry to do this to you. We are way beyond our time, I guess because of the 30-minute break that we took a little earlier; and I'm just wondering what the situation with the tapes might be. Could we maybe take a break and come back at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, fine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are going to have to take just one hour when we come back because of -- okay. We'll take a break and come back at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, we have a map in front of us now, and I think that the map is the one you drew on last time you were in court. So we'd like to go back to that one, and would you do the same thing that you did in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we'll need the assistance of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the direction the tram was going and where you were, to draw into the map where you were when you heard the shots for the first time, approximately. So can you show us the place on this map where the tram was hit and where you were hit. Can you do that on this map?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one question at a time. First of all, maybe if you can start with the direction the tram was moving, let her show that, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just asking that because I was talking to the court officer to see whether we've zoomed in sufficiently because once we get going we can't zoom in any more. So that's why I wanted to ask her whether she could see all that on this part of the map as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, can you draw in the direction the tram was moving in, and the street was Zmaja od Bosna Street. Just an arrow showing the direction.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The tram was moving this way. You want an arrow, so this would be it, then. It was moving from Bascarsija to Cengic Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And would you place a number 1 by the arrow, and that is the direction the tram was taking.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll place the 1 by the top of the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, before you heard the shots, do you know where the previous tram stop was? Do you remember? If not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember where that was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, using this same map, can you mark in with a number 2, if you're able to, that is to say, recognise the buildings that can remind you where the tram was when you heard the shots.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was between these two museums, the M. That's the crossroads, and there's a school here, so that's the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you place the number 2 there, then, please.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the two Ms are the museums, two museums marked with the letter M.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said that this was a very short space of time, so could you place an X where you think the tram was hit.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to determine that because we were moving, and when I felt danger, I knelt down and the glass was above my head, and I was looking at the tin of the tram. So it's difficult for me to say. It's difficult to determine time at times like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us roughly how far after the crossroads where the museums are this was, roughly, at what distance?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean where I heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where the bullets hit the tram.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say, but it was roughly somewhere in between those two points. The tram was moving. It was a short space of time, and then you had the whole situation and my experiences of it, and it's difficult to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. But can we say, then, that this was, let's say -- well, from the crossroads, could you give us the number of minutes? Ten seconds, five, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I really can't. Please understand me, time was very relative during moments like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Now, you said that you heard the shots. Did you see the direction from which the shots came when the tram was hit, or prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I was facing the Marsal Tito barracks, as they were called, so I was facing north.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, could you put a 3 there.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll put a 3. That's the direction that I was facing. I was looking that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on you said that you came to the conclusion that the shots had come from the direction of Grbavica. Did you conclude that judging by where the tram was hit, the direction from which the tram was hit, that the bullets came?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had an entrance-exit wound. I still have that. So the bullet, as I'm standing, entered this way and exited that way, which means that it came from my back and exited towards my face, where my face was turned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, can we note that the witness is showing the area of her left elbow, with an entrance and exit wound above the elbow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't above the elbow. It was all below the elbow, the exit and entrance wound, both below the elbow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. We'll just place that on the record, that it was below the elbow. Well, she has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you now mark on this map where you think the shots came from, from this area that you said was Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says "Grbavica," so that's where that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- well, we see the Miljacka river there, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just pause between my question and your answer, please, Witness. Anyway, this section from the Miljacka river towards the museum, which forces controlled that area? Do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The river was the border, the separation line in that part of town, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So do you perhaps know which forces controlled the area from Hrasno, the Hrasno area? I assume you know where Hrasno is. So do you know who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Hrasno settlement -- yes, I will pause between question and answer. Thank you. The Hrasno settlement was controlled by the BH army, but the front lines were there, so I can't be specific. But I do know that the settlement and the houses there was where the Bosnia-Herzegovina army was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear. The circle around Grbavica, would you place a "G" there, the letter "G" for Grbavica; and then place an "H" for Hrasno settlement so that we can mark that area too.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This settlement, Hrasno, does it incorporate -- well, actually, could you draw a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where the separation lines were there; but otherwise, Hrasno, the name of the settlement, is written up on the map. It says "Hrasno," and I'll underline that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And another thing that I'd like you to mark into the map, do you know where Vrbanja Most is, the bridge, and if so, would you mark that.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Vrbanja" here, so that's the bridge, and I've just put an X there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've put an X by Vrbanja bridge, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It looks like an X.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'd like to tender this map, but I'd like to discuss the map further, so may we leave it up on our screens. I know that there was a problem if the map is taken away from the screen. It's a problem to get it back again, so leave the map there, please. And I'd like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. But you still have questions to ask on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map on the screen is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked map becomes Exhibit D1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we can agree, madam, Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, that the Miljacka river was the separation line, the demarcation line between the two territories, controlled on the one side by the Army of Republika Srpska and on the other, the BH army, in this part of town, the part where the tram was hit.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the tram was full or empty? Now, you've already said that, but I'd like it on the record: How many people were in the tram? Is it an articulated tram, the big one, or not, or a smaller one? Do you happen to remember?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. It was an articulated tram, a big one, four doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there a lot of people in the tram? Was it full?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the reaction in the tram of the people when the shots rang out?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The people began to throw themselves down onto the ground. I crouched down, too; I knelt down, and the people who were by the steps went into this area because it was a more protected area, where the steps were, by the doors, and the doors were facing the number 3 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember -- well, if I can put it this way: Were there screams, shouts? Were the passengers raising their voices and shouting?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But anyway, you said you were facing the right-hand side -- you were on the right-hand side of the tram facing the direction the tram was taking, right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, facing number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the previous trial you were shown a document, and I don't want to put the document before you because it was admitted into evidence. It is an UNPROFOR document, a report which said that when this incident took place, that there was a conflict at Vrbanja Most, Vrbanja bridge, between the two -- well, warring parties, and that it was with respect to that incident that the BH army was cautioned and the Army of Republika Srpska too. You're familiar with the document. We don't need to bring it up again, and it's already in evidence, anyway. But at any rate, you cannot actually tell me since you were facing the right-hand side whether you saw any events going on on the left-hand side before the shots that you heard.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After those first shots, there was a lot of commotion. People were shouting. There was noise, loud noise. Now, this noise, this commotion, was that straight after the first shots or only when you felt that the tram had been hit?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Dragomir Milosevic trial, on page 1666, you said that you cannot be 100 per cent sure whether the first burst of gunfire came from the territory covered by the BH army or the territory covered by the Army of Republika Srpska. That's what you said at the time. Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have it on record anyway. Would you tell me -- well, just a moment, please. Let me take a moment. You were -- or rather, do you remember after the shots were fired, how long did the tram continue running before it stopped and you were able to get out?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say but not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it stopped --

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was covered by the buildings, but as soon as a car arrived, they took me to the emergency ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we remove this exhibit here, Mrs. Mulaosmanovic, counsel for the Defence asked you a question, and this was at page 70, lines 6 to 8. He said, "Just pause between my question and answer, Witness. This section between the Miljacka river and towards the museum, which forces controlled that area? Do you happen to know?" And that question was not answered. Do you have an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The river was the separation line, so it was the -- it was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The area between the museums was under the control -- that was -- listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just this section between the Miljacka river and towards the museum, which forces controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were the forces of the BH army, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you know whether the Grbavica area was controlled by any army?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Grbavica was under the control of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So the Serbian army was in between two sections of the Bosnian army because you said, also, Hrasno was under the control of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that part of town where Grbavica is located. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you about Hrasno, where you've marked "H."

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under whose control was that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA CEHAJIC-MULAOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions? Any questions here? Do you have any questions arising from my questions? No. Have we admitted this map? Yes, we have. Thank you very much. Ma'am, thank you so much for coming. This brings us to the end of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber just wants to take this opportunity to thank you for coming to testify. You are now excused. You may stand down and travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not have another witness available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for that, Mr. Saxon. Just one or two housekeeping matters. The Chamber would like to give an oral decision. Could the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution will have one witness available tomorrow. It will likely have two witnesses available for Wednesday. If those witnesses finish on Wednesday, then the Prosecution would have no more witnesses available for Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Wednesday is the 8th. If we do sit at all on Wednesday -- I just wanted to mention in advance to the parties that the Appeal Chamber has asked to use our time to deliver a judgement in the Martic appeals case, and if we have to sit, we are going to have to sit after they have delivered that judgement, okay? Thank you so much. That's all I had for housekeeping. Court stands adjourned until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: WITNESS:  CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.26 p.m.,
